lead: Most screens today are raster displays: a grid of picture cells called pixels, visited row by row many times each second. An older random scan display draws only the lines in its display list, like a pen tracing a drawing. The designs differ in memory, cost and flicker. They explain why a monitor needs a frame buffer and a refresh rate. Only a few universities teach this display hardware in depth. The idea sits under every image on a phone, laptop or TV.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.2 for pixels versus stored shapes.

blocks.text: In a raster scan system the screen is a grid of picture cells called pixels. The display visits the grid row by row, left to right, then returns to the top. One horizontal pass is a scan line. The return from bottom right to top left is vertical retrace. One complete screen image is a frame. The number of complete redraws each second is the refresh rate, in hertz (Hz); 60 Hz means 60 passes per second.

On a cathode ray tube (CRT), an electron gun at the back sends a beam toward the screen. Deflection coils bend the beam across and down. The beam hits phosphor, which glows briefly. The picture must be redrawn before it fades; too slow a refresh gives flicker. Interlacing splits one frame into two fields: even rows, then odd rows. It halves the signal rate but can show combing on motion.

The bitmap lives in a frame buffer, memory holding a colour for every pixel. A display processor turns geometry from the CPU into pixels. A video controller reads the buffer in row order and sends the signal to the monitor. Frame size is image width in pixels × image height in pixels × bytes per pixel. The figure shows the chain.

sections.h3: Random scan: drawing only the listed lines

blocks.text: A random scan display, also called a vector or calligraphic display, stores a display list of line segments. The electron beam moves to one endpoint, draws that line, then jumps to the next. It draws only listed lines and leaves blank space untouched. The order is arbitrary; random scan does not mean random pixels.

The beam still comes from an electron gun and is bent by deflection coils in a CRT. Each line is a continuous stroke, so wireframe edges look smooth and line art needs little memory. Every listed line is redrawn on every refresh. A long list takes longer, so refresh rate falls and flicker appears. Random scan is poor for filled regions and photographs. Precision deflection hardware can cost more than a simple raster monitor. Typical uses are oscilloscopes and wireframe CAD.

An LCD (liquid crystal display) is a flat panel with a grid of cells and a backlight. Each cell controls how much light passes; red, green and blue filters form subpixels. The panel stores pixel values and refreshes them row by row, so it is a raster system without an electron beam. An OLED (organic light-emitting diode) display has pixels that emit their own light. Black pixels switch off, so contrast is high and dark scenes use less power. Both still need a frame buffer and a video controller.

LCD is usually cheaper at large sizes; OLED costs more but gives deeper black. A CRT can flicker at low refresh; LCD backlights can flicker under some dimming methods, and OLED under pulse-width dimming. A fixed pixel grid is sharpest at native resolution and blurs when scaled. High refresh reduces motion blur. Random scan has no fixed grid, so lines stay smooth, but it cannot store a photograph efficiently.

figure.caption: The frame buffer holds all 786,432 pixels of the 1024 × 768 screen at 3 bytes each, so 2,359,296 bytes or 2.25 MiB. The video controller re-reads that whole buffer 60 times a second — 141.6 MB/s — and sends the rows to the monitor, which is why the picture does not fade.

spec.title: Raster scan path
spec.aria: A five-block chain from CPU through display processor to a frame buffer holding 2,359,296 bytes, then a video controller that reads the buffer 60 times a second at 141.6 MB/s and drives a 1024 by 768 monitor.

examples.question: A raster display has 1024 × 768 pixels and 24 bits per pixel. (a) Find the frame buffer size in bytes and in mebibytes (1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes). (b) At a refresh rate of 60 Hz, find the byte rate the video controller must read, in bytes per second and in megabytes per second (1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes).
examples.answer: Frame buffer = 2,359,296 bytes = 2.25 MiB; controller read rate = 141,557,760 bytes/s = 141.55776 MB/s, about 141.6 MB/s.
examples.check:
width = 1024
height = 768
bpp = 24
refresh = 60
pixels = width * height
bytes_per_pixel = bpp // 8
frame_bytes = pixels * bytes_per_pixel
frame_mib = frame_bytes / 1048576
rate_bytes = frame_bytes * refresh
rate_mb = rate_bytes / 1000000
print(pixels)
print(bytes_per_pixel)
print(frame_bytes)
print(frame_mib)
print(rate_bytes)
print(rate_mb)

traps: Raster scan visits every pixel row; it does not follow a line endpoint to endpoint.
Refresh rate is screen redraws per second, not animation frame rate.
24 bits per pixel equals 3 bytes per pixel, not 24 bytes.
Interlacing draws two fields; it is not a higher native resolution.
Random scan means display-list order, not random pixel addresses.

quiz.q: Define refresh rate and give its unit.
quiz.a: Complete screen redraws per second; unit hertz (Hz).

quiz.q: Why does a raster CRT need a frame buffer?
quiz.a: It stores every pixel; the video controller rereads it for each refresh without the CPU rebuilding the picture.

quiz.q: An 800 × 600 raster display uses 8 bits per pixel. Find the frame buffer size in bytes and in KiB (1 KiB = 1024 bytes).
At 75 Hz, what byte rate does the display in the previous question need?
Why does a random scan display flicker when its display list grows?
quiz.a: Each refresh redraws all listed lines; more lines take longer, so the refresh rate falls.

quiz.q: A CAD user draws thin wireframe parts; a photo editor works on filled images. Which display type suits each, and why?
quiz.a: Random scan suits wireframes: only listed lines, smooth edges, little memory. Raster suits photos: every pixel stores colour and fills.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern panels add variable refresh rate (FreeSync, G-Sync), high dynamic range and subpixel layouts that affect text sharpness. Phone OLEDs often share subpixels to raise lifetime. Search next for frame buffer bandwidth, display serial interface (DSI) and variable refresh rate; e-ink is a bistable panel that needs no continuous refresh for a still page.
